title: Electromagnetism, optics and waves, relativity, quantum physics

chapters.title: Quantum foundations
chapters.what: Light comes in quanta of energy hf (Planck, Einstein) and matter has a wavelength h/p (de Broglie). Both are waves and particles: the black-body spectrum, the photoelectric effect, Compton scattering and electron diffraction all demand it.
chapters.looks: Spectra and energy curves (2D); the Planck surface over wavelength and temperature, or the photon–electron momentum triangle (3D).
chapters.change: Heat the black body: the peak slides to shorter wavelength and the area grows as T⁴.
chapters.use: Thermal cameras, star temperatures, solar cells, X-ray imaging, electron microscopes.
misc: Brighter light gives more photoelectrons, not faster ones.
A photon has momentum but no mass.

examples.title: The Sun's spectrum peaks in the visible
examples.world: A 5778 K surface peaks near 502 nm (Wien's law).

examples.title: Thermal cameras see people
examples.world: Skin at 310 K glows near 9.3 µm, in the long-wave infrared.

examples.title: The Sun's surface power
examples.world: σT⁴ = 63 MW per square metre of the Sun's surface.

examples.title: The photoelectric effect in sodium
examples.world: UV at 1.5 × 10¹⁵ Hz ejects electrons with up to 3.92 eV from sodium (φ = 2.28 eV).

examples.title: Compton scattering at 90°
examples.world: X-rays scattered at 90° lengthen by the Compton wavelength, 2.43 pm.

examples.title: Davisson–Germer: electrons diffract
examples.world: 54 V electrons (λ = 0.167 nm) diffracted from nickel like X-rays.

chapters.title: The Schrödinger equation
chapters.what: A particle is described by a wavefunction ψ(x); |ψ|² is the probability density. In a potential well only certain energies fit (quantisation), and a particle can leak through a barrier it could not classically climb (tunnelling).
chapters.looks: The potential, the energy levels and each wavefunction drawn at its level (2D); |ψ(x,t)|² of a two-state superposition sloshing in time (3D).
chapters.change: Shrink the well: every level rises as 1/a² (quantum dots change colour with size).
chapters.use: Quantum dots, lasers, the scanning tunnelling microscope, molecular vibrations, flash memory.
misc: The wavefunction is not a smeared-out particle.
Tunnelling does not violate energy conservation.

examples.title: The particle in a box
examples.world: The ground energy of a box of width 1 is π² (ħ = 2m = 1); the finite-difference solver gets 9.8696.

examples.title: Levels grow as n²
examples.world: E₂/E₁ = 4 in a box: conjugated dye molecules absorb at the gap.

examples.title: The harmonic oscillator: equal spacing
examples.world: Molecular vibrations absorb infrared at one frequency because the levels are evenly spaced.

examples.title: Quantum dots: smaller is bluer
examples.world: Halving the box quadruples the energy: Brus (1984) explained the size-dependent colour.

examples.title: Tunnelling through a barrier
examples.world: The STM current depends exponentially on the gap (Binnig et al. 1982).

examples.title: A double well
examples.world: Ammonia's nitrogen tunnels between two wells: the tunnelling splitting drove the first maser.

examples.title: A finite well
examples.world: Only a finite number of bound states fit in a well of finite depth.

chapters.title: Operators and quantum states
chapters.what: Observables are operators; the possible results of a measurement are their eigenvalues, and the probabilities come from projecting the state onto the eigenstates. A spin-½ state is a point on the Bloch sphere.
maths: P(\uparrow_{\hat m})=\tfrac12(1+\hat n\cdot\hat m),\quad [\hat x,\hat p]=i\hbar
chapters.looks: The state vector and measurement axis with the probability bar (2D); the Bloch sphere with the precession cone (3D).
chapters.change: Rotate the measurement axis: the probability of 'up' follows (1 + cos α)/2; press ▶ to precess the state.
chapters.use: MRI, atomic clocks, quantum computing qubits, Stern–Gerlach magnets.
misc: A measurement result is always an eigenvalue, never an average.
The Bloch sphere angle θ is twice the Hilbert-space angle.

examples.title: Stern–Gerlach on an x-spin
examples.world: A spin along x measured along z gives up or down with 50 % each.

expect.label: P(↑ along the measurement axis) = (1 + n·m)/2
P(↑ along the measurement axis) = (1 + n·m)/2

examples.title: The expectation value ⟨σz⟩
examples.world: For θ = 120° the average of many z measurements is cos 120° = −0.5.

examples.title: Larmor precession: the basis of MRI
examples.world: In a field along z the spin precesses at constant θ; press ▶.

examples.title: Energy eigenvalues of the Hamiltonian
examples.world: A box of width 2 has ground energy π²/4: the eigenvalue of Ĥ.
